 Tracking the K-12 student population in NYC 1 
Executive Summary 
Over the last decade, New York City’s K-12 student population has decreased 
dramatically. There are significantly fewer students across the City than there were a 
decade ago and NYC Public Schools (NYCPS) have seen a steep drop in enrollment. In 
SY2025-26, NYCPS saw its steepest drop in enrollment since the pandemic, losing 21,793 
students, a three percent year-to-year decline of students. 
There are many factors that impact school enrollment, from individual family decisions to 
population-level macro-trends. During the timeframe examined in this report, the number 
of children born each year in NYC has declined steadily, which is one contributing factor to 
decreasing school enrollment. Other factors like families with children leaving NYC and 
shifts in immigration patterns have also likely had an impact on NYCPS enrollment. This 
resource presents foundational school enrollment data to help New Yorkers understand 
the state of the student population in our education system.

• K-12 enrollment in NYCPS declined by 19% from SY2013-14 to SY2025-26, and 
enrollment is projected to continue to decline.

a decrease of 21,793 students, a 3% year-to-year decline. 
• The decline in NYCPS enrollment largely reflects a broader decrease in the number 
of school-aged children in New York City – not increased enrollment in other school

Dear Mr. Amodei: 
 
I write to urge Anthropic to pause its planned initial public offering (IPO) until the company 
fully and transparently addresses the artificial intelligence (AI) safety, governance, and 
development pace concerns it has raised. Instead of proceeding headlong with its IPO, the 
company should focus its energies on addressing these unprecedented risks. 
 
Anthropic and five other companies recently signed a “morally binding” accord with the 
White House, which is insufficient to meet the moment. Before going public, the company 
should prioritize addressing the myriad safety concerns surrounding AI threats and 
establishing a governance regime that matches the seriousness of the concerns being 
raised by you as well as industry researchers, policymakers, and the public. The demands 
of preparing for a public offering diverts resources and attention from this very necessary 
work. 
 
As Comptroller of the City of New York, I serve as investment adviser to, and custodian and 
a trustee of, the New York City pension funds, which have over $325 billion in assets and 
constitute one of the largest public pension systems in the United States. 
 
In recent weeks, Anthropic has issued unusually direct public statements acknowledging 
that the pace of frontier-model capability development may now exceed society’s capacity 
to understand and control the resulting systems. You have disclosed that unchecked 
recursive self-improvement could outrun human oversight. In your September 12 essay, 
“We Must Pace the Frontier,” you stated: “…over the last few months, I have become 
convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence ... We must slow 
the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models.” 
 
Despite these heightened safety warnings and broad calls for greater caution across the 
industry, Anthropic reportedly continues to push forward an IPO that could value the 
company at approximately $2 trillion.

Dear Secretary Kennedy, 
 
As the elected Comptroller of the City of New York, I write in strong opposition to the 
Department of Health and Human Services’ (the Department) proposed rule changes to 
the Head Start Program and Performance Standards (the Standards), published in the 
Federal Register on August 7, 2026. 
 
Done properly, with care and precision, regulatory reform can be a useful tool for 
modernizing public systems and improving outcomes. Well-considered changes to 
regulations can also increase government efficiency, safeguard public funds, and ensure 
that public programs produce strong results. The proposed changes to the Standards 
would do the opposite. 
 
Since it first launched in 1965, Head Start has afforded our youngest New Yorkers living in 
poverty and their families the opportunity to receive high-quality early childhood education 
and services that put them on a path to academic, social, and financial success. Head 
Start does this by serving the rich mix of New York City’s families. According to data 
retrieved from the Head Start Program Information Report (PIR), in 2025, there were more 
than 20,000 children and more than 800 pregnant women enrolled in Head Start in New 
York City from all racial and ethnic backgrounds. The largest groups identified as Hispanic 
or Latino (29%), Black or African American (27%), White (non-Hispanic or Latino) (25%), 
Biracial or Multi-Racial (11%), Asian (6%), and American Indian/Alaska Native (2%). 
 
I am deeply concerned that the proposed changes eliminate a significant portion of the 
Standards that form the backbone of Head Start’s program effectiveness. These changes

full_text:
The DOHMH Washington Heights Clinic is currently closed.  DOHMH does not currently have a re-opening date for this location. 

DOHMH is still providing various services in this area to support its residents. For example, DOHMH's Bureau of Immunization supports a Continued Access to Vaccination site located in Washington Heights (Ryan Health Wadsworth) to provide vaccinations for un/underinsured children and adults who reside in this area. Additionally, so far in 2025 the DOHMH Bureau of Maternal, Infant, and Reproductive Health (BMIRH) served 302 Washington Heights residents through its various home visiting programs 252 via the Newborn Home Visiting Program and 50 through the New Family Program). In the last 9 months, BMIRH's Newborn Home Visiting Program has attended and provided resources at 7 community baby showers in the Washington Heights and Inwood neighborhoods. On multiple occasions, this program provided items such as onesies, bibs, pack n plays, cribs, etc. to hundreds of families in attendance. The Nurse Family Partnership program regularly conducts clinician outreach and participates in family health events in this area. Additionally, DOHMH has 9 SBHCs in Washington Heights and the Inwood area, operated by Children's Aid Society, NYP, and the Community Healthcare Network. The DOHMH Bureau of Hepatitis, HIV, and Sexually Transmitted Infections also runs several HIV prevention programs in the area with partner organizations such as NYP/Columbia, Alliance for Positive Change, and OnPoint NYC, providing mental health services including psychotherapy, family counseling, patient navigation, therapeutic groups specializing in youth and young adults living with HIV, a multi-level antiretroviral treatment adherence support program integrated into HIV care management to promote viral load suppression, substance abuse, and other supportive services to meet and address health care needs and improve individual health outcomes.

Located at 600 West 168 Street, the DOHMH Washington Heights Center is an important piece of the City's Upper Manhattan health service network. On the floors operated by the DOHMH, we have public services that range from free and confidential testing and treatment for tuberculosis, and insurance enrollment, and co-located community based service providers. The City also recognizes there is a strong interest to do more to connect these services to the community and are excited for the prospect of working on that with the Council Member to do that work
- The City will work with the Council Member's office to develop an outreach strategy to inform and attract more eligible residents of Manhattan Community Board 12 to take advantage of the health services on site. Outreach to include health fairs, targeted neighborhood advertisement (including Get Covered NYC and other medical campaigns as funding allows), and promoting available services through Columbia University's Get Health Heights coalition.

title: Bay Street: Improve Village Hall at Tappen Park
summary: The Village Hall roof reconstruction project was completed in May 2025. RFEI responses for a creative use of the space are currently being reviewed and will inform a potential future RFP for a concession.
full_text:
The Village Hall roof reconstruction project was completed in May 2025. RFEI responses for a creative use of the space are currently being reviewed and will inform a potential future RFP for a concession.

Tappen Park's Village Hall building is a historic landmark that was built in 1889 and first
operated as the home of the Village of Edgewater's municipal and civic activities. Now vacant
and in a state of disrepair, the building most recently housed municipal offices and a health
clinic. The City commits $5.7 million to repair the building's roof and transfer jurisdiction of the
structure to NYC Parks. Once repair work is complete, NYC Parks intends to activate the building
with a concession, programming space and public restrooms.

title: East Harlem: Expand the Harlem River Greenway Link to connect 125th and 132nd St
summary: Construction began in July 2024 and is anticipated to be complete in 2028.
full_text:
Construction began in July 2024 and is anticipated to be complete in 2028.

The waterfront between E125th and E132nd streets provides a rare opportunity to build a new 7 block long waterfront park. It will provide an exciting amenity for East Harlem residents and will complete one of the last remaining gaps in the Manhattan Waterfront Greenway; today, East Harlem is essentially cut off from the Manhattan Greenway. The bulkhead and waterfront platform will be repaired/replaced and a new park constructed on top. The community has joined The New York City Department of Parks and Recreation (DPR)to design the new park, which is anticipated to include bicycle and pedestrian paths, play and picnic areas, landscaping, and other recreational amenities. The City has already committed $18M to be used towards waterfront repair work between E125th-E132nd Streets, and is committing an additional $83M to be used towards further open space development between E125th and E132nd Streets.

title: Inwood: Rebuild Monsignor Kett Playground as an intergenerational park and destination
summary: NYC Parks completed the playground construction in July 2023 and anticipates public bathroom construction completion in Summer 2025.
full_text:
NYC Parks completed the playground construction in July 2023 and anticipates public bathroom construction completion in Summer 2025.

Monsignor Kett Playground is a key open space for the residents of NYCHA's Dyckman Houses and Inwood. The site's basketball courts are very heavily used for tournaments and free play. The facility has not seen a major capital upgrade in decades and lacks a year-round comfort station. The City will fund a comprehensive renovation of Monsignor Kett Playground, potentially including high-grade basketball courts with amenities for league play, an intergenerational fitness area, a new year-round comfort station, and connections from the park to the streetscape through Parks-Without-Borders perimeter treatments. NYC Parks will lead a public design process to re-envision the space and will include the Council Member, CB 12, Dyckman Houses, the leagues and sports groups that utilize the site, and other stakeholders.

title: Inwood: Renovate Inwood Hill Park Soccer Field #1 (Dyckman Fields), including installation of new water service
summary: Construction of the new turf field began in July 2024 and construction completion is anticipated for Summer 2025.
full_text:
Construction of the new turf field began in July 2024 and construction completion is anticipated for Summer 2025.

Dyckman Fields Soccer Field #1 is a heavily used recreational amenity. The lack of water service to Dyckman Fields has led to soil compaction at this soccer field resulting in significant bare spots in the lawn and frequent dust bowl conditions, reducing public access due to flooding during wet conditions, and resulting in further erosion. The City will fund NYC Parks to reconstruct Soccer Field #1 to create a high-caliber, safe athletic facility for league and recreation use. A key component of the project will also include installation of water service, which will increase usability.

title: Jerome: Renovate and Expand Grant Avenue Park
summary: Construction of Grant Avenue Park is anticipated to be completed in Fall 2025.
full_text:
Construction of Grant Avenue Park is anticipated to be completed in Fall 2025.

The development of Grant Park offers an opportunity to expand open space and create a sizable neighborhood park for this community. This capital project will expand the existing park by closing Grant Avenue between 169th and 170th Streets, responding to strong community desire for increased open space and recreational opportunities. The full renovation is expected to include roadbed conversion, infrastructure work, lawn area, and 2-3 sports courts.
